title: Real Addition is Associative
theorem_text:
The operation of addition on the set of real numbers $\R$ is associative:
$\forall x, y, z \in \R: x + \paren {y + z} = \paren {x + y} + z$
proof_text:
From the definition, the real numbers are the set of all equivalence classes $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers.
Let $x = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}, y = \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}, z = \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$, where $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$, $\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$ and $\eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$ are such equivalence classes.
From the definition of real addition, $x + y$ is defined as $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} + \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n + y_n} } {}$.
Thus we have:
$$x + \paren {y + z} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} + \paren {\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} + \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {} }$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} + \eqclass {\sequence {y_n + z_n} } {}$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n + \paren {y_n + z_n} } } {}$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {\paren {x_n + y_n} + z_n} } {}$$
Rational Addition is Associative
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n + y_n} } {} + \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$$
$$= \paren {\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} + \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} } + \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$$
$$= \paren {x + y} + z$$
review_reason: Addition of real equivalence classes is represented by termwise addition. Rational associativity makes the representatives agree at every index.

title: Real Multiplication is Associative
theorem_text:
The operation of multiplication on the set of real numbers $\R$ is associative:
$\forall x, y, z \in \R: x \times \paren {y \times z} = \paren {x \times y} \times z$
proof_text:
From the definition, the real numbers are the set of all equivalence classes $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers.
Let $x = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}, y = \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}, z = \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$, where $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$, $\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$ and $\eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$ are such equivalence classes.
From the definition of real multiplication, $x \times y$ is defined as $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times y_n} } {}$.
Thus we have:
$$x \times \paren {y \times z} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \paren {\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {} }$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n \times z_n} } {}$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times \paren {y_n \times z_n} } } {}$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {\paren {x_n \times y_n} \times z_n} } {}$$
Rational Multiplication is Associative
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times y_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$$
$$= \paren {\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} } \times \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$$
$$= \paren {x \times y} \times z$$
review_reason: Termwise multiplication of representatives reduces both bracketings to the same sequence by associativity of rational multiplication.

title: Real Multiplication is Commutative
theorem_text:
The operation of multiplication on the set of real numbers $\R$ is commutative:
$\forall x, y \in \R: x \times y = y \times x$
proof_text:
From the definition, the real numbers are the set of all equivalence classes $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers.
Let $x = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}, y = \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$, where $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ and $\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$ are such equivalence classes.
From the definition of real multiplication, $x \times y$ is defined as $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times y_n} } {}$.
Thus we have:
$$x \times y = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times y_n} } {}$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {y_n \times n_n} } {}$$
Rational Multiplication is Commutative
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$$
$$= y \times x$$
review_reason: Rational commutativity swaps the two factors at each index, so the product classes agree. The unexplained n_n in one display is a typo for the x_n appearing before and after it.

title: Rational Numbers form Metric Space
theorem_text:
Let $\Q$ be the set of all rational numbers.
Let $d: \Q \times \Q \to \R$ be defined as:
$\map d {x_1, x_2} = \size {x_1 - x_2}$
where $\size x$ is the absolute value of $x$.
Then $d$ is a metric on $\Q$ and so $\struct {\Q, d}$ is a metric space.
proof_text:
From the definition of absolute value:
$\size {x_1 - x_2} = \sqrt {\paren {x_1 - x_2}^2}$
This is the same as the Euclidean metric.
This is shown in Euclidean Metric on Real Vector Space is Metric to be a metric.
From Rational Numbers form Vector Space, it follows that the set of all rational numbers is a 1-dimensional Euclidean space.
review_reason: Being one-dimensional over Q does not make Q a one-dimensional real vector space, so the stated application of the Euclidean vector-space theorem to Q is unjustified. Restricting the real metric to Q would suffice.

title: Rational Numbers form Vector Space
theorem_text:
Let $\Q$ be the set of rational numbers.
Then the $\Q$-module $\Q^n$ is a vector space.
It follows directly, by setting $n = 1$, that the $\Q$-module $\Q$ itself can also be regarded as a vector space.
proof_text:
From the definition, a vector space is a unitary module whose scalar ring is a field.
From Rational Numbers form Field, we have that $\Q$ is a field.
So the $\Q$-module $\Q^n$ fits the description.
review_reason: The given coordinate module is unital and its scalar ring Q is a field, so it is a vector space by definition, including when n=1.

title: Limit of (Cosine (X) - 1) over X
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \frac {\map \cos x - 1} x = 0$
proof_text:
This proof assumes the truth of the Derivative of Cosine Function:
From Cosine of Zero is One:
$\cos 0 = 1$
From Derivative of Cosine Function:
$D_x \left({\cos x}\right) = - \sin x$
and by Derivative of Constant:
$D_x \left({-1}\right) = 0$
So by Sum Rule for Derivatives:
$D_x \left({\cos x - 1}\right) = - \sin x$
By Sine of Zero is Zero:
$\sin 0 = 0$
From Derivative of Identity Function:
$D_x \left({x}\right) = 1$
Thus L'Hôpital's Rule applies and so:
$\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \frac {\cos x - 1} x = \lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \frac {-\sin x} 1 = \frac {-0} 1 = 0$
review_reason: With the cited cosine derivative available, the numerator and denominator both vanish at zero and the derivative ratio −sin(x) tends to zero. L'Hôpital's rule applies.

title: Limit of (Cosine (X) - 1) over X
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \frac {\map \cos x - 1} x = 0$
proof_text:
$$\lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \ \frac {\cos x - 1} x = \lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \ \frac {\left({\cos x - 1}\right) \left({\cos x + 1}\right)} {x \left({\cos x + 1}\right)}$$
$$= \lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \ \frac {\cos^2 x - 1} {x \left({\cos x + 1}\right)}$$
$$= \lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \ \frac {-\sin^2 x} {x  \left({\cos x + 1}\right)}$$
Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine
$$= \left({\lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \ \frac {\sin x} x}\right) \left({\lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \ \frac {-\sin x} {\cos x + 1} }\right)$$
Product Rule for Limits of Functions
$$= 1 \times \left({\lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \ \frac{-\sin x} {\cos x + 1} }\right)$$
Limit of Sine of X over X
$$= \frac {\lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \left({- \sin x}\right)} {\lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \left({\cos x + 1}\right)}$$
Quotient Rule for Limits of Functions
$$= \frac 0 2$$
$$= 0$$
review_reason: Multiplication by the conjugate expression gives (sin x/x) times −sin x/(1+cos x); the factors tend to 1 and 0 respectively.

title: Limit of (Cosine (X) - 1) over X
theorem_text: $\displaystyle \lim_{x \mathop \to 0} \frac {\map \cos x - 1} x = 0$
proof_text:
$$\frac {\cos x - 1} x = \frac {\cos x - \cos 0} x$$
Cosine of Zero is One
$$\to \left.{\dfrac {\mathrm d} {\mathrm dx} \cos x}\right \vert_{x \mathop = 0}$$
as $x \to 0$, from definition of derivative at a point
$$= \sin x \vert_{x \mathop = 0}$$
Derivative of Cosine Function
$$= 0$$
Sine of Zero is Zero
review_reason: The quotient is the cosine difference quotient at zero. The derivative is −sin x; its missing minus sign in the displayed evaluation makes no difference at zero.

title: Real Multiplication Distributes over Addition
theorem_text:
The operation of multiplication on the set of real numbers $\R$ is distributive over the operation of addition:
$\forall x, y, z \in \R:$
$x \times \paren {y + z} = x \times y + x \times z$
$\paren {y + z} \times x = y \times x + z \times x$
proof_text:
From the definition, the real numbers are the set of all equivalence classes $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers.
Let $x = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}, y = \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}, z = \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$, where $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$, $\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$ and $\eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {}$ are such equivalence classes.
From the definition of real multiplication, $x \times y$ is defined as:
$\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times y_n} } {}$
From the definition of real addition, $x + y$ is defined as:
$\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} + \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n + y_n} } {}$
Thus:
$$x \times \paren {y + z} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \paren {\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} + \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {} }$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {x_n + y_n} } {}$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times \paren {y_n + z_n} } } {}$$
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {\paren {x_n \times y_n} + \paren {x_n \times z_n} } } {}$$
Rational Multiplication Distributes over Addition
$$= \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times y_n} } {} + \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times z_n} } {}$$
$$= \paren {\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} } + \paren {\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {z_n} } {} }$$
$$= \paren {x \times y} + \paren {x \times z}$$
By Real Addition is Commutative and Real Multiplication is Commutative, it follows that:
$\paren {y + z} \times x = \paren {y \times x} + \paren {z \times x}$
review_reason: Rational distributivity gives the termwise identity in the representatives of the three classes; commutativity then gives right distributivity. One intermediate sum writes x_n+y_n where the surrounding lines require y_n+z_n.

title: Finite Subset of Metric Space has no Limit Points
theorem_text:
Let $M = \left({A, d}\right)$ be a metric space.
Let $X \subseteq A$ such that $X$ is finite.
Then $X$ has no limit points.
proof_text:
Let $x \in X$.
From Point in Finite Metric Space is Isolated, $x$ is an isolated point.
The result follows by definition of isolated point:
$x$ is an isolated point if and only if $x$ is not a limit point.
review_reason: Isolating each member of X only excludes limit points inside X. The proof never excludes ambient points outside X, for which a neighborhood disjoint from the finite set is needed.

title: Point in Finite Metric Space is Isolated
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space.
Let $X \subseteq A$ such that $X$ is finite.
Let $x \in X$.
Then $x$ is isolated in $X$.
proof_text:
A Metric Space is Hausdorff.
Therefore Point in Finite Hausdorff Space is Isolated can be applied.
Hence the result.
review_reason: The metric space is Hausdorff and the cited finite-subset result for Hausdorff spaces gives isolation of the given point in X.

title: Point in Finite Hausdorff Space is Isolated
theorem_text:
Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a Hausdorff space.
Let $X \subseteq S$ such that $X$ is finite.
Let $x \in X$.
Then $x$ is isolated in $X$.
proof_text:
Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space.
Let $X \subseteq T$ be finite.
From Separation Properties Preserved in Subspace, it follows that $\left({X, \tau_X}\right)$ is also a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space.
From $T_2$ Space is $T_1$ Space it follows that $\left({X, \tau_X}\right)$ is a $T_1$ (Fréchet) space.
From Finite $T_1$ Space is Discrete, it follows that $\left({X, \tau_X}\right)$ is a discrete space.
The result follows from Topological Space is Discrete iff All Points are Isolated.
review_reason: The finite subspace inherits Hausdorff separation, hence is T1 and discrete. Its singleton neighborhoods give the required isolation.

title: Primes of form Power Less One
theorem_text:
Let $m, n \in \N_{>0}$ be natural numbers.
Let $m^n - 1$ be prime.
Then $m = 2$ and $n$ is prime.
proof_text:
First we note that by Integer Less One divides Power Less One:
$\paren {m - 1} \divides \paren {m^n - 1}$
where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.
Thus $m^n - 1$ is composite for all $m \in \Z: m > 2$.
Let $m = 2$, and consider $2^n - 1$.
Suppose $n$ is composite.
Then $n = r s$ where $r, s \in \Z_{> 1}$.
Then by the corollary to Integer Less One divides Power Less One:
$\paren {2^r - 1} \divides \paren {2^{r s} - 1}$
Thus if $n$ is composite, then so is $2^n - 1$.
So $2^n - 1$ can be prime only when $n$ is prime.
review_reason: For n=1 the displayed divisor m−1 equals the entire number, so compositeness does not follow. For example, 3^1−1 is prime.

title: First Subsequence Rule
theorem_text:
Let $T = \left({A, \tau}\right)$ be a Hausdorff space.
Let $\left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle$ be a sequence in $T$.
Suppose $\left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle$ has two convergent subsequences with different limit.
Then $\left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle$ is divergent.
proof_text:
From Convergent Sequence in Hausdorff Space has Unique Limit, if $\left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle$ is convergent in a Hausdorff space it has exactly one limit.
From Limit of Subsequence equals Limit of Sequence, any subsequence of a convergent sequence must have the same limit.
So, if a sequence has two convergent subsequences with different limit, it must in fact be divergent.
review_reason: If the sequence converged, both subsequences would converge to its limit, unique by Hausdorff separation. Distinct subsequence limits contradict this.

title: Divisibility by 7
theorem_text:
An integer $X$ with $n$ digits ($X_0$ in the ones place, $X_1$ in the tens place, and so on) is divisible by $7$ if and only if:
$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {3^i X_i}$ is divisible by $7$.
proof_text:
$$X = 10^0 X_0 + 10^1 X_1 + \cdots + 10^{n - 1} X_{n-1}$$
$$= \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} 10^i X_i$$
$$= \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {10^i - 3^i + 3^i} X_i$$
$$= \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {\paren {10^i - 3^i} X_i} + \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {3^i X_i}$$
From Difference of Two Powers, $10^i - 3^i$ always produces a number divisible by $7$.
Thus the first addend is always divisible by $7$.
So $X$ will be divisible by $7$ if and only if the second addend is divisible by $7$.
Hence the result.
review_reason: Replacing each place weight 10^i by 3^i leaves a difference divisible by 7. Summing preserves the residue, and a sign on the original integer does not affect divisibility.

title: Finite Subspace of Dense-in-itself Metric Space is not Open
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space that is dense-in-itself.
Let $U$ be a finite subset of $A$.
Then $U$ is not an open set of $M$.
proof_text:
Let $U = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$.
Aiming for a contradiction, suppose that $U$ is open.
Let:
$\displaystyle D = \min_{i \mathop \ne j} \map d {x_i, x_j}$
Let $x_j \in U$.
Consider the open ball $\map {B_{D/2}} {x_j}$ of $x_j$.
From Open Ball of Metric Space is Open Set, $\map {B_{D/2}} {x_j}$ is an open set.
Then from Finite Intersection of Open Sets of Metric Space is Open, we can see that $U \cap B_{D/2}$ is also an open set.
However, we have that:
$D/2 < \displaystyle \min_{i \mathop \ne j} \map d {x_i, x_j}$
Thus the open ball $\map {B_{D/2}} {x_j}$ is simply the singleton $\set {x_j}$.
But then $x_j$ is an isolated point of $M$.
This contradicts the fact that $M$ is dense-in-itself.
So in fact, $U$ cannot be open.
The result follows.
review_reason: The proof assumes U has points and a minimum pairwise distance. The empty finite set is open in every metric space. Also it is the intersection of the displayed ball with U that isolates a point, not necessarily the ambient ball.

title: Composite Number has Prime Factor not Greater Than its Square Root
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \N$ and $n = p_1 \times p_2 \times \cdots \times p_j$, $j \ge 2$, where $p_1, \ldots, p_j \in \Bbb P$ are prime factors of $n$.
Then $\exists p_i \in \Bbb P$ such that $p_i \le \sqrt n$.
That is, if $n \in \N$ is composite, then $n$ has a prime factor $p \le \sqrt n$.
proof_text:
Let $n$ be composite such that $n \ge 0$.
From Composite Number has Two Divisors Less Than It, we can write $n = a b$ where $a, b \in \Z$ and $1 < a, b < n$.
without loss of generality, suppose that $a \le b$.
Let $a > \sqrt n$.
Then $b \ge a > \sqrt n$.
However, if $b \ge a > \sqrt n$ is true, then:
$n = a b > \sqrt n \sqrt n > n$
This is clearly a contradiction.
So:
$a \le \sqrt n$
From Positive Integer Greater than 1 has Prime Divisor it follows that there is some prime $p$ which divides $a$.
From Absolute Value of Integer is not less than Divisors, we have that $p \le a$ and so:
$p \le \sqrt n$
From Divisor Relation on Positive Integers is Partial Ordering:
$p \divides n$
Hence the result.
review_reason: The smaller factor of n=ab is at most √n, since otherwise ab>n. A prime divisor of that factor divides n and is no larger; the displayed √n·√n is equal to n.

title: Sum Over Divisors Equals Sum Over Quotients
theorem_text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer.
Let $f: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ be a mapping on the positive integers.
Let $\displaystyle \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f d$ be the sum of $\map f d$ over the divisors of $n$.
Then:
$\displaystyle \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f d = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f {\frac n d}$.
proof_text:
If $d$ is a divisor of $n$ then $d \times \dfrac n d = n$ and so $\dfrac n d$ is also a divisor of $n$.
Therefore if $d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_r$ are all the divisors of $n$, then so are $\dfrac n {d_1}, \dfrac n {d_2}, \ldots, \dfrac n {d_r}$, except in a different order.
Hence:
$$\sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f {\frac n d} = \map f {\frac n {d_1} } + \map f {\frac n {d_2} } + \cdots + \map f {\frac n {d_r} }$$
$$= \map f {d_1} + \map f {d_2} + \cdots + \map f {d_r}$$
$$= \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f d$$
review_reason: Dividing n by a positive divisor permutes its positive divisors because applying the operation twice returns the original divisor. Reindexing preserves the sum.

title: Sigma Function of Power of Prime
theorem_text:
Let $n = p^k$ be the power of a prime number $p$.
Let $\map \sigma n$ be the sigma function of $n$.
That is, let $\map \sigma n$ be the sum of all positive divisors of $n$.
Then:
$\map \sigma n = \dfrac {p^{k + 1} - 1} {p - 1}$
proof_text:
From Divisors of Power of Prime, the divisors of $n = p^k$ are $1, p, p^2, \ldots, p^{k - 1}, p^k$.
Hence from Sum of Geometric Sequence:
$\map \sigma {p^k} = 1 + p + p^2 + \cdots + p^{k - 1} + p^k = \dfrac {p^{k + 1} - 1} {p - 1}$
review_reason: The positive divisors of p^k are precisely its powers from 0 through k. Summing that geometric progression gives the quotient claimed.

title: Tau of Power of Prime
theorem_text:
Let $n = p^k$ be the power of a prime number $p$.
Let $\tau \left({n}\right)$ be the $\tau$ function of $n$.
That is, let $\tau \left({n}\right)$ be the number of positive divisors of $n$.
Then $\tau \left({n}\right) = k + 1$.
proof_text:
From Divisors of Power of Prime, the divisors of $n = p^k$ are $1, p, p^2, \ldots, p^{k-1}, p^k$.
There are $k + 1$ of them.
Hence the result.
review_reason: The listed divisors are the distinct powers p^0 through p^k, so counting their exponents gives k+1.

title: Sum Over Divisors of Multiplicative Function
theorem_text:
Let $f: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ be a multiplicative function.
Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$.
Let $\displaystyle \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f d$ be the sum over the divisors of $n$.
Then $\displaystyle \map F n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f d$ is also a multiplicative function.
proof_text:
Let $\displaystyle \map F n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map f d$.
Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}: m \perp n$.
Then by definition:
$\displaystyle \map F {m n} = \sum_{d \mathop \divides m n} \map f d$
The divisors of $m n$ are of the form $d = r s$ where $r$ and $s$ are divisors of $m$ and $n$ respectively, from Divisors of Product of Coprime Integers.
It is noted that $r \perp s$, otherwise any common divisor of $r$ and $s$ would be a common divisor of $m$ and $n$.
Therefore:
$\displaystyle \map F {m n} = \sum_{r \mathop \divides m, \ s \mathop \divides n} \map f {r s}$
So, as $f$ is multiplicative:
$\displaystyle \map F {m n} = \sum_{r \mathop \divides m, \ s \mathop \divides n} \map f r \map f s$
But at the same time:
$\displaystyle \map F m \map F n = \paren {\sum_{r \mathop \divides m} \map f r} \paren {\sum_{s \mathop \divides n} \map f s}$
Multiplying out the product on the right-hand side, $\map F {m n}$ and $\map F m \map F n$ are seen to be the same.
review_reason: For coprime inputs the divisors of the product are in bijection with pairs of their divisors, themselves coprime. Multiplicativity turns the double sum into the product of the two sums.

title: Divisors of Product of Coprime Integers
theorem_text:
Let $a \divides b c$, where $b \perp c$.
Then $\tuple {r, s}$ satisfying:
$a = r s$, where $r \divides b$ and $s \divides c$
is unique up to absolute value with:
$\size r = \gcd \set {a, b}$
$\size s = \gcd \set {a, c}$
proof_text:
By Divisor of Product, there exists $\tuple {r, s}$ satisfying:
$r \divides b$
$s \divides c$
$r s = a$
We have:
$r, s \divides a$
By definition of GCD:
$\gcd \set {a, b} \divides r$
$\gcd \set {a, c} \divides s$
By Absolute Value of Integer is not less than Divisors:
$\gcd \set {a, b} \le \size r$
$\gcd \set {a, c} \le \size s$
We also have:
$$\size {r s} \ge \gcd \set {a, b} \gcd \set {a, c}$$
$$= \gcd \set {a, b c}$$
GCD with One Fixed Argument is Multiplicative Function
$$= \size a$$
GCD of Integer and Divisor
$$= \size {r s}$$
This forces both inequalities to be equalities, i.e.:
$\size r = \gcd \set {a, b}$
$\size s = \gcd \set {a, c}$
Hence $\tuple {r, s}$ is unique up to absolute value.
review_reason: From r dividing a and b one obtains r dividing gcd(a,b), the reverse of the stated premise. The analogous assertion for s and the resulting bounds are unsupported.

title: Tau Function is Multiplicative
theorem_text:
The divisor counting function:
$\displaystyle \tau: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}: \map \tau n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} 1$
is multiplicative.
proof_text:
Let $f_1: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ be the constant function:
$\forall n \in \Z_{>0}: \map {f_1} n = 1$
Thus we have:
$\displaystyle \map \tau n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} 1 = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map {f_1} d$
But from Unity Function is Completely Multiplicative, $f_1$ is multiplicative.
The result follows from Sum Over Divisors of Multiplicative Function.
review_reason: The divisor count sums the constant-one multiplicative function over the divisors, exactly the preceding divisor-sum multiplicativity theorem.

title: Sigma Function is Multiplicative
theorem_text:
The sigma function:
$\displaystyle \sigma: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}: \sigma \left({n}\right) = \sum_{d \mathop \backslash n} d$
is multiplicative.
proof_text:
Let $I_{\Z_{>0}}: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ be the identity function:
$\forall n \in \Z_{>0}: \map {I_{\Z_{>0} } } n = n$
Thus we have:
$\displaystyle \map \sigma n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} d = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} \map {I_{\Z_{>0} } } d$
But from Identity Function is Completely Multiplicative, $I_{\Z_{>0} }$ is multiplicative.
The result follows from Sum Over Divisors of Multiplicative Function.
review_reason: The sum of divisors is the divisor sum of the identity function, which is completely multiplicative. The cited divisor-sum closure result applies.

title: Sigma Function is Multiplicative
theorem_text:
The sigma function:
$\displaystyle \sigma: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}: \sigma \left({n}\right) = \sum_{d \mathop \backslash n} d$
is multiplicative.
proof_text:
Let $a, b$ be coprime integers.
Because $a$ and $b$ have no common divisor, the divisors of $a b$ are integers of the form $a_i b_j$, where $a_i$ is a divisor of $a$ and $b_j$ is a divisor of $b$.
That is, any divisor $d$ of $a b$ is in the form:
$d = a_i b_j$
in a unique way, where $a_i \divides a$ and $b_j \divides b$.
We can list the divisors of $a$ and $b$ as
$1, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a$
and:
$1, b_1, b_2, \ldots, b$
and so their $\sigma$ function values are:
$\displaystyle \map \sigma a = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r a_i$
$\displaystyle \map \sigma b = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^s b_j$
Consider all divisors of $a b$ with the same $a_i$.
Their sum is:
$$\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^s a_i b_j = a_i \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^s b_j$$
$$= a_i \map \sigma b$$
Summing for all $a_i$:
$$\map \sigma {a b} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r \paren {a_i \map \sigma b}$$
$$= \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r a_i} \map \sigma b$$
$$= \map \sigma a \map \sigma b$$
review_reason: For positive coprime a and b, every positive divisor of ab is a unique product of respective divisors. Summing over those pairs factors the sum into σ(a)σ(b).

title: Primes of form Power of Two plus One
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number.
Let $2^n + 1$ be prime.
Then $n = 2^k$ for some natural number $k$.
proof_text:
Suppose $n$ has an odd divisor apart from $1$.
Then $n$ can be expressed as $n = \paren {2 r + 1} s$.
So:
$$2^n + 1 = 2^{\paren {2 r + 1} s} + 1$$
$$= \paren {2^s}^{\paren {2 r + 1} } + 1^{\paren {2 r + 1} }$$
$$= \paren {2^s + 1} \paren {2^{2 r s} - 2^{\paren {2 r - 1} s} + 2^{\paren {2 r - 2} s} - \cdots - 2^s + 1}$$
Sum of Odd Positive Powers
and so $2^n + 1$ is not prime.
Hence $2^n + 1$ can be prime only if $n$ has only even divisors.
That is, if $n = 2^k$ for some natural number $k$.
review_reason: The factorization only forces compositeness when the factors are nontrivial, which fails at n=0. Then 2^0+1=2 is prime, yet 0 is no power of 2.

title: Primes of form Power of Two plus One
theorem_text:
Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number.
Let $2^n + 1$ be prime.
Then $n = 2^k$ for some natural number $k$.
proof_text:
A specific instance of Primes of form Power plus One:
$q^n + 1$ is prime only if:
$(1): \quad q$ is even
and
$(2): \quad n$ is of the form $2^k$ for some positive integer $k$.
As $2$ is even, the result applies.
review_reason: The cited positive-exponent result does not cover n=0, which gives the prime 2, and its demand for positive k even excludes n=1. Substituting the even base 2 does not fix those range errors.

title: Integer has Multiplicative Order Modulo n iff Coprime to n
theorem_text:
Let $a$ and $n$ be integers.
Let the multiplicative order of $a$ modulo $n$ exist.
Then $a \perp n$, that is, $a$ and $n$ are coprime.
proof_text:
Necessary Condition
Suppose $c \in \Z_{>0}$ is the multiplicative order of $a$ modulo $n$.
Then by definition:
$a^c \equiv 1 \pmod n$
Hence, by definition, $a^c = k n + 1$ for some $k \in \Z$.
Thus:
$a r + n s = 1$
where $r = a^{c-1}$ and $s = -k$.
It follows from Integer Combination of Coprime Integers that $a$ and $n$ are coprime.
Sufficient Condition
Suppose $a \perp n$.
Then by Euler's Theorem:
$a^{\phi \left({n}\right)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$
where $\phi \left({n}\right)$ is the Euler Phi Function of $n$.
Hence the multiplicative order of $a$ modulo $n$ exists, by taking $c = \phi \left({n}\right)$.
review_reason: For the implication actually stated, a positive exponent giving residue 1 supplies the Bézout identity 1=a·a^(c−1)−kn. That suffices for coprimality without the extra converse argument.

title: Sum of Infinite Geometric Sequence
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a standard number field, that is $\Q$, $\R$ or $\C$.
Let $z \in S$.
Let $\size z < 1$, where $\size z$ denotes:
:the absolute value of $z$, for real and rational $z$
:the complex modulus of $z$ for complex $z$.
Then $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty z^n$ converges absolutely to $\dfrac 1 {1 - z}$.
proof_text:
By the Chain Rule for Derivatives and the corollary to $n$th Derivative of Reciprocal of $m$th Power:
$\dfrac {\d^n} {\d z^n} \dfrac 1 {1 - z} = \dfrac {n!} {\paren {1 - z}^{n + 1}}$
Thus the Maclaurin series expansion of $\dfrac 1 {1 - z}$ is:
$\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {z^n} {n!} \dfrac {n!} {\paren {1 - 0}^{n + 1}}$
whence the result.
review_reason: Computing the Taylor coefficients identifies the formal series but does not justify its convergence to the function on the unit disk or absolute convergence. A remainder estimate or analytic convergence theorem is needed.

title: Order of Möbius Function
theorem_text:
Let $\mu$ denote the Möbius function .
Then:
$\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop \le N} \map \mu n = \map o N$
where $o$ denotes little-o notation.
proof_text:
Let $\map \Re z$ be the real part of a complex variable $z$.
By Dirichlet Series is Analytic, the Riemann zeta function is analytic.
By Trivial Zeroes of Riemann Zeta Function are Even Negative Integers, the Riemann zeta function has no zeroes in $\map \Re z > 1$.
Thus the reciprocal of the Riemann zeta function is analytic in $\map \Re z > 1$.
By Reciprocal of Riemann Zeta Function, this means that $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \map \mu n n^{-z}$ converges to an analytic function in $\map \Re z > 1$.
By taking $a_n = \mu \left({n}\right)$ in Ingham's Theorem on Convergent Dirichlet Series:
$\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac {\map \mu n} {n^z}$ converges for $\map \Re z \ge 1$.
Taking $z = 1$, we are given a convergent sum:
$\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac {\map \mu n} n$
Clearly:
$\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^N \frac {\map \mu n} n \ge \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^N \frac {\map \mu n} N$
but:
$\displaystyle \lim_{N \mathop \to \infty} \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^N \frac {\map \mu n} n = \lim_{z \mathop \to 1} \frac 1 {\map \zeta z}$
Since Harmonic Series is Divergent, $\dfrac 1 {\map \zeta z}$ goes to $0$ by Reciprocal of Null Sequence.
Hence also:
$\displaystyle \lim_{N \mathop \to \infty} \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^N \frac {\map \mu n} N = 0$
review_reason: Analyticity in Re(z)>1 alone does not justify the boundary convergence attributed to Ingham. The final comparison also treats the signed Möbius coefficients as though each were nonnegative.
